lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: What is the difference between [==|double equals] and [===|triple equals] in JavaScript?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: [==|Double equals] converts the types first, then compares. [===|Triple equals] never converts.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Watch what happens.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: When the types differ, [==|double equals] converts them first, usually to numbers.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Zero [==|double equals] false is true, because false is converted to the number zero.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: With [===|triple equals], a number and a boolean are different types, so the answer is false.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The same happens with the string one and the number one.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: And null [==|double equals] undefined is true, but with [===|triple equals] it is false.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So is triple equals always safe?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Not quite. [NaN|Not a number] is never equal to anything, not even itself, with either operator.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: To check for it, use [Number.isNaN|Number dot is N a N], or [Object.is|Object dot is].

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Objects are compared by reference, so two separate empty arrays are never equal.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: Is there a classic trap?

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Yes. Null [==|double equals] zero is false, but null [>=|greater than or equal to] zero is true.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The comparison operators convert null to zero. But [==|double equals] treats null in a special way.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: So use [===|triple equals] by default.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: The one common exception is [x == null|x double equals null].

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: It is true for null and for undefined, and nothing else.

lines.speaker: sam
lines.text: So, triple equals, and double equals only for null checks.

lines.speaker: byte
lines.text: Exactly. That is your interview answer.
